title: Motivation and emotion
note: Motivation is what starts, directs and sustains behavior; it can come from inside (interest, satisfaction) or outside (pay, praise). Emotion is a relatively intense response to an event, involving bodily arousal, thought and expression. Theories of emotion differ mainly on the order and role of arousal and interpretation.

read.title: When a reward backfires
text: Some activities we do because they are interesting or satisfying in themselves. That is intrinsic motivation. Others we do for something outside the activity, such as pay, grades or praise. That is extrinsic motivation. Both are useful, but they can interact in surprising ways.

In the overjustification effect, adding an outside reward to an activity a person already enjoys can reduce their interest in it. Picture a child who loves to draw. If adults start paying her for every drawing, she may begin to see drawing as work done for money. When the payments stop, she may draw less than before.

The effect depends on the kind of reward. Tangible rewards, like money or prizes, tend to undermine intrinsic motivation more than intangible ones, like sincere praise. Expected rewards do more harm than surprise rewards, because the expectation changes how the person explains their own behavior.

None of this means rewards are bad. They can help a person start a task they do not yet value, and they are fair payment for work. The lesson is to protect the interest that already exists: praise effort and progress, and give learners real choices, so the reason for doing the task stays their own.

q.q: In the overjustification effect, what happens to intrinsic motivation?
o: It can weaken when an outside reward is added

q.q: Which reward is most likely to undermine interest, according to the reading?

o: Praise effort and give learners real choices
